01 / DECIDE

Choose a musical move.

The planner proposes a track, a cue point, and a transition using known state and analysis.

02 / SEND

Translate it into MIDI.

A predictable executor turns the plan into bounded commands for the host.

03 / PERFORM

Move the actual controls.

Mixxx applies the action through its shared control system. The UI and audio follow.

04 / CONFIRM

See what really happened.

Feedback updates the AI’s state, including changes you make by hand.

Why this direction

Own the intelligence.
Build on a working instrument.

01

Spend the effort on DJing.

Mixxx gives us a starting point for decks, mixing, effects, and a visible interface. Our work can focus on the decisions and execution that make an AI DJ worth using.

02

Make every move inspectable.

Open source lets us trace a MIDI command into the host and close gaps when needed. A moving fader and returned state give us something concrete to test.

03

Give the brain room to move.

The AI lives in its own process. Keeping MIDI at the boundary creates a path from two local programs to a separate controller device.

Source-backed starting point: Mixxx’s shared control system and controller scripting. The complete AI integration still needs to be built and tested.
One architecture. Two stages.

Prove it here.
Move it later.

For now, everything runs on this computer. Virtual MIDI connects the local AI DJ process to Mixxx, with a separate return path for feedback.

The ambition

A route to every feature.

Full control remains the goal. We earn that claim feature by feature: send the action, observe the outcome, and show the result.

START WITH THE PERFORMANCE SURFACE

Get the core set working.

Map existing Mixxx controls and test them in both directions. Begin with two decks and a small set of actions we can verify.

Play & cueCrossfaderVolume & EQTempo & syncLoops & effects
EXTEND WHERE THE HOST NEEDS HELP

Close the important gaps.

Reliable track selection, richer state, and modal settings need more than a button press. Custom MIDI SysEx messages can carry the protocol; host extensions supply missing operations.

Stable track identityLoad confirmationMetadataSettings workflows
The engineering boundaries we are keeping honest

MIDI carries control and feedback, not the music. Shared controls provide a strong starting point, but “every feature” is not yet verified. The inspected legacy Mixxx MIDI handler ignores incoming beat clock, so the initial timing approach uses host sync and quantized behaviors, with measurements. Another DJ application would need a separate adapter and capability review. Pi inference and audio performance remain future tests.

Read the architecture plan, feature coverage, or source findings for the details behind this direction.

The path to a useful DJ

Earn autonomy, one set at a time.

Start with a repeatable performance. Add musical judgment once the hands, eyes, and takeover controls work.

01 / NEXTLOCAL

Connect the decks.

Build the virtual MIDI mapping. Send simple commands and receive state changes from Mixxx.

PROOF: The UI moves. Feedback agrees.
02LOCAL

Perform a transition.

Execute a known two-deck sequence. Confirm each step and handle manual takeover and reconnects.

PROOF: A repeatable, reviewable mix.
03LOCAL

Add musical judgment.

Let the AI propose tracks and transitions. Expand and validate the full feature inventory.

PROOF: Good decisions, dependable execution.
04LATER

Put it in a box.

Move the controller to a Pi. Validate physical MIDI, power recovery, and performance on real hardware.

PROOF: The local behavior travels.

The first win is small.
The direction is much bigger.

Two tracks. One clean transition. Visible control and feedback you can trust. That gives us a foundation for an AI DJ that can actually perform.
